# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Empirical dynamic models (EDMs) have been shown to capture population dynamics of short-lived species better than traditional stock assessment methods, including surplus production and age-structured models.  Prediction accuracy of recently developed EDMs for brown shrimp abundance ($R^2$=0.70, out-of-sample $R^2$=0.36) vastly exceeds that of previous assessment models built in the Gulf of America. The Gulf shrimp fishery was once extremely profitable until emerging aquaculture trimmed costs and drove global prices down, resulting in reduced revenue and fleet consolidation. Attempts have been made through the years to segment the domestic market and push prices back up so the Gulf shrimp fleet can cover trawling costs. Strategies include premium labeling in the form of seafood certification or country of origin labeling, allowing consumers to distinguish between domestic and imported shrimp.  Here, we estimated size-specific harvest rates using observed ex-vessel and fuel prices ($R^2$=0.65) and re-fit the base EDM using these estimates.  Then, we simulated realistic economic projection scenarios including (1) baseline [2020-2022 average price], (2) continued competition with farmed imports [25\% decrease in price], (3) tariff-induced increase [25\% increase in price], (4) premium label product increase [50\% increase in price], and (5) harvest rate at brown shrimp maximum sustainable yield identified in the latest stock assessment for three fuel price scenarios [\$1.50, baseline 2020-22 average, and \$4.00].  The price EDM had improved prediction accuracy for brown shrimp abundance (out-of-sample $R^2$=0.43). No scenario resulted in a depleted population and the premium-label scenario resulted in over \$250 million increase in annual revenue.

**Keywords:** fisheries management, population dynamics, short-lived species, nonlinear dynamics
